---
title: "Choosing a Python API"
subtitle: "Start with the question, then select the model that includes its costs."
---

MLSys·im separates specifications, equations, and the solvers that combine them.
The same engine serves every textbook volume. Choosing an API depends on the
physical question, not on which volume introduces it.

## Choose the calculation

| Question | Start here | What the result represents |
|:--|:--|:--|
| How do compute and memory bandwidth constrain one device? | `Engine.solve()` | A generic Roofline profile with declared traffic and overhead approximations |
| How do prompt length, KV storage, and batch size affect token generation? | `ServingModel().solve()` | Separate prefill and decode estimates with KV-aware memory accounting |
| Does training fit, or how does a fleet scale? | `TrainingMemoryModel` or `DistributedModel` | Training-state capacity or distributed training performance |
| How do named workload and hardware choices perform against a latency target? | `Scenario(...).evaluate()` | A composed feasibility, performance, and annual economics scorecard |
| What does one equation imply? | A function in `mlsysim.physics` | A reusable calculation with an explicit unit and modeling contract |

The [solver guide](solver-guide.qmd) maps additional questions to solvers. The
[resolver guide](models-and-solvers.qmd) explains forward models, inverse solvers,
and optimizers. These categories describe different calculations; using a more
specialized class only helps when its assumptions match the question.

## A generic single-device profile

Import the main entry point and registries from `mlsysim`. This example evaluates
one batch of a vision model. Its efficiency is an assumed compute-capacity
fraction, not a measured end-to-end utilization.

```{python}
#| label: api-engine-example
from mlsysim import Engine, Hardware, Models

profile = Engine.solve(
    model=Models.Vision.ResNet50,
    hardware=Hardware.Cloud.H100,
    batch_size=8,
    precision="fp16",
    efficiency=0.5,  # Assumed compute efficiency for this example.
)
print(f"Fits modeled memory: {profile.feasible}")
print(f"Batch latency: {profile.latency.to('ms'):~.3f}")
print(f"Limiting resource: {profile.bottleneck}")
```

`Engine.solve()` returns a `PerformanceProfile`. Its `latency` is per batch;
`throughput` divides batch size by that latency. A feasibility flag checks the
modeled footprint, which does not reserve all production runtime workspaces.

For a language model, the generic engine uses an activation-traffic approximation.
It does not become KV-aware autoregressive serving simply because the workload
is a transformer. A sweep through this API cannot establish a serving engine's
inter-token latency or continuous-batching capacity.

## KV-aware language-model serving

Import specialized classes from `mlsysim.solvers`. `ServingModel` keeps prompt
prefill and decode separate. Decode compares compute time with weight and KV
traffic time, then adds the configured layer overhead. Either compute or memory
can limit the estimate.

```{python}
#| label: api-serving-example
from mlsysim import Hardware, Models
from mlsysim.solvers import ServingModel

serving = ServingModel().solve(
    model=Models.Language.Llama3_8B,
    hardware=Hardware.Cloud.H100,
    seq_len=2048,
    batch_size=1,
    precision="fp16",
    efficiency=0.5,  # Derates compute; it does not derate memory bandwidth.
)
print(f"Fits modeled memory: {serving.feasible}")
print(f"Prefill estimate: {serving.ttft.to('ms'):~.3f}")
print(f"Decode step estimate: {serving.itl.to('ms'):~.3f}")
print(f"KV storage: {serving.kv_cache_size.to('GB'):~.3f}")
```

Here `seq_len` sets the modeled context length. `itl` is a decode step under
those assumptions; it is not a request's total latency divided by its output
length. The default prefill model is compute based. These estimates do not
include every kernel, allocator, scheduling, or multi-device communication cost.
The [serving reference](api/solvers.ServingModel.qmd) documents the supported
options and exclusions.

## A named scenario and scorecard

A `Scenario` binds a workload, target system, and declared constraints so a
calculation can be reused. This example adds an illustrative latency target to a
vision workload; the target is a local assumption, not a hardware specification.

```{python}
#| label: api-scenario-example
from mlsysim import Hardware, Models, Q_, Scenario

scenario = Scenario(
    name="Vision latency exercise",
    description="Evaluate a vision batch against an illustrative latency target.",
    workload=Models.Vision.ResNet50,
    system=Hardware.Cloud.H100,
    sla_latency=Q_("10 ms"),
)
scorecard = scenario.evaluate(batch_size=8, precision="fp16")
print(f"Feasibility: {scorecard.feasibility.status}")
print(f"Performance: {scorecard.performance.status}")
print(scorecard.performance.summary)
```

The current generic `Scenario.evaluate()` uses `SingleNodeModel` for one device
and `DistributedModel` for a fleet. It does **not** select `ServingModel` when the
workload is a language model. Its feasibility level checks weight residency and
any configured input data rate; its performance level checks the latency target.
Its macro level uses annual economics defaults. It is not a check of every
constraint exposed elsewhere in the package. For explicit serving costs,
training-memory breakdowns, or custom economics assumptions, call those solvers
directly and compose their results.

`Scenario` is the class for a local case. `Scenarios` is the registry of named,
reusable cases and analytical inputs. Inspect an entry's type and documentation:
not every registry entry has the generic class's `evaluate()` method.

## Follow a result into the code

| Layer | Source location | What to inspect |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Specifications | `hardware/`, `models/`, `systems/`, `infrastructure/` | Typed fields, units, and provenance for selected inputs |
| Equations | `physics/` | Reusable formulas, assumptions, exclusions, and references |
| Composition | `engine/solvers/` | How a domain solver combines equations and accounts for costs |
| Scenario definitions | `engine/scenario_definitions/` | Typed inputs and their calculations, grouped by domain |
| Named configurations | `engine/scenario_catalog/` | Reusable choices of inputs exposed through `Scenarios` |
| Outputs | `engine/result_types/` | Result schemas, units, and constraint traces in the same domains |
| Presentation | `fmt/`, `viz/`, `cli/`, `labs/` | Formatting and interaction around those results |

Some domain-specific calculations live directly in a solver or a private shared
helper. Follow its source link rather than assuming every equation is in
`physics/`. The [modeling conventions](modeling-conventions.qmd) describe the
calculation documentation contract; the [API reference](api/index.qmd) is built
from the package docstrings.

The [code walkthrough](code-walkthrough.qmd) follows one serving case through
these layers. Browse [scenarios by domain](api/scenario-domains.qmd) for related
calculations, or use [the alphabetical index](api/scenario-index.qmd) for a known
class name.

Use the public imports shown above in textbook cells and applications. Internal
paths explain where implementation lives, but callers do not need to depend on
private helpers or the layout beneath `engine/solvers/`. This separation allows
internal cleanup while preserving the public entry points.

`engine/scenario_types.py`, `engine/scenarios.py`, and `engine/results.py`
preserve the established imports. Their definitions live in the domain packages
listed above; the compatibility modules do not own a second implementation.
